text: Sometimes you can't avoid walking through a result set one row at a time inside procedural code, and that's what a cursor is for. All four platforms share the exact same concept — declare it, open it, fetch rows in a loop, close it when you're done — but the actual syntax, and especially how you detect you're out of rows, is genuinely different on each one.

T-SQL first. Declare cursor for select product id, name from production dot product, open cur, fetch next from cur into at product id, at name, while at at fetch status equals zero, begin, print at name, fetch next from cur into the same variables again, end, close cur, deallocate cur. Notice that fetch next appears twice — once to prime the status before the loop even starts, and again inside the loop body. Forget either one and the loop either never runs or never stops.

PL/SQL's explicit cursor form swaps that status check for a cursor attribute. Cursor cur is select product id, name from products, open cur, loop, fetch cur into v underscore id, v underscore name, exit when cur percent notfound, dbms output put line v underscore name, end loop, close cur. Percent notfound replaces at at fetch status. But this is really the long way to do it in PL/SQL.

Here's the ergonomics win worth remembering. PL/SQL's cursor for-loop: for rec in open paren select product id, name from products close paren loop, dbms output put line rec dot name, end loop. That's it. Open, fetch every row, and close — all handled automatically. No manual bookkeeping at all, and most real PL/SQL code uses exactly this form unless it specifically needs manual control.

MySQL takes a third approach entirely. Declare done int default false, declare cur cursor for select name from products, declare continue handler for not found set done equals true, open cur, read underscore loop colon loop, fetch cur into v underscore name, if done then leave read underscore loop, end if, end loop, close cur. There's no percent notfound and no at at fetch status — instead you declare a handler ahead of time that quietly sets a flag the moment fetch runs dry, and you check that flag yourself.

One more thing worth knowing: PostgreSQL's PL slash pgsql supports the same for rec in select loop idiom as Oracle, with the same automatic open-fetch-close convenience — it's the idiomatic way to iterate there too, not manual cursor management. Next lesson: error handling, where T-SQL's try-catch, PL/SQL's exception blocks, and MySQL's noticeably more awkward handler model all come head to head. See you there.
